To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the evolution of the neurofibrillary pathology is the same in both nondementing and demented subjects, and that the hyperphosphorylation of tau protein is an early event in the formation of neurofibrils.
the evolution of neurofibrilary tangles in neurons is the same in both nondementing and Alzheimer's disease patients.

(i) neurofibrillary degeneration is a common process in both nondementing and dementing brains; (ii) hyperphosphorylation of tau protein precedes the formation of neurofibrils; (iii) neurofibrils appear as granules of hyperphosphorilated tau, which are subsequently transformed into short paired helical filamets and, finally, into straight filaments, which become organized in bundles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural and functional characterization of the neuronal cytoskeleton.
the study of the ultrastructural evolution of neurons with neurof fibrillary tangles in aging and Alzheimer’s disease.
the study of the ultrastructural aspects of neurofilamentous degeneration in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and normal aging.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the formation of paired helical and/or straight filaments in neurons of nondemented aged individuals is the same as that occurring in neurons of demented patients.

neurofibrillary degeneration in the aging and in Alzheimer’s disease is an active process of the neuron, which is initiated by an increase of phosphorylation of the microtubule-associated protein tau, followed by a progressive aggregation of this protein in paired helical and in straight filaments.
the neurofibrillary changes in Alzheimer disease are not a primary event, but rather a secondary consequence of neuronal dysfunction and death.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evolution of neurofibrils in neurons with neurofilary tangles is similar in both nondementer and Alzheimer's disease.
the evolution of neurofibrillar tangles in the brains of nondemented and Alzheimer's disease patients is the same.
the neurofibrillary pathology is the same in both aging and Alzheimer's brains, thus indicating that aging is a necessary but not a sufficient condition to develop the Alzheimer's disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
neurofibrillary pathology is a process, and not a single event.
the formation of the paired helical and the straight filaments in the neurons is a continuous process.
neurofibrillary degeneration occurs in both nondement and demented aged brains and that the process is the same.
